AfriScan · DR Congo · Emprises and mining perimeters

Know what has changed inside your right of way or concession

AfriScan finds and counts structures, pits, disturbed ground and tracks along power lines, railways and roads, and inside mining perimeters in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Each structure is measured to your route or boundary, tied to the image it was found on, checked by an analyst and delivered as GIS files and a PDF report. The work is done remotely, from satellite imagery.

Request a proposal Working with us in the DRC
  • 25 m each sideThe emprise of high-voltage lines
  • 800 m · 1,000 mThe distances in Mining Code art. 279
  • Every 500 mRated for encroachment density

Our published sample is from Mozambique: the route of a high-pressure gas pipeline, with its 100 m band, on a Copernicus Sentinel-2 scene of 2 August 2026. Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data 2026.

The rules behind the work Loi n° 10/014 on civil aviation, art. 58 bis · Arrêté interministériel n° 0021 of 29 October 1993 (servitudes) · Loi n° 14/011 on electricity · Mining Code, arts 279 and 281 · Loi n° 17/001 on subcontracting · Décret n° 14/019 (ESIA) · IFC Performance Standard 5

What the texts say

Distances set in Congolese law, measured structure by structure

Three sets of rules give a survey in the DRC its widths: the servitudes, the electricity law and the Mining Code. Checked against the published texts on 27 September 2026. A summary of the public rules for orientation; it is not legal advice.

Servitudes. Arrêté interministériel n° 0021 of 29 October 1993 lists among the servitudes “les emprises des lignes de haute tension sur une distance de 25 mètres de part et d’autre” (the emprises of high-voltage lines, 25 metres on each side) and railway emprises “de 5 à 50 mètres suivant catégories” (5 to 50 metres, depending on category). It prohibits “toute occupation, toute construction et tout lotissement” there: any occupation, construction or subdivision (art. 2).

Electricity. Loi n° 14/011 of 17 June 2014 on the electricity sector penalises anyone who builds on or under power lines or occupies the emprises of the State’s public electrical installations (art. 125). It also says that overhead conductors crossing a land concession do not stop the holder fencing or building there: a servitude of passage for maintenance remains, and the holder gives three months’ notice before building (arts 108 and 109).

Mining. Under the Mining Code, a mining right holder may not occupy, without the consent of the owner or lawful occupant, land within 1,000 metres of houses or buildings or within 800 metres of cultivated fields (art. 279, as amended in 2018). These distances protect the people who live and farm there; they do not make a house near a mine unlawful.

AfriScan measures each structure it records against these distances, or against the ones you set.

Who decides

Whether a structure is permitted is for you and the competent authorities to decide. How the 1993 arrêté fits with art. 108 of the electricity law, which does not stop a land holder building under a line that crosses the concession, is a point for counsel.

Power-line emprises · Rail and road emprises · Mining perimeters

What you receive

A dated register your land, HSE and GIS teams can use

  • Structures counted by distance band, for example 0–10, 10–25 and 25–50 m on each side of a line, and by 500 m segment, each segment rated for encroachment density. It is a counting rule, not a safety rating.
  • Each structure’s distance to the route or boundary, its chainage and its coordinates in WGS84 and UTM.
  • The imagery named, and dated where the source gives a capture date.
  • Changes since the previous survey, flagged automatically and confirmed by an analyst, with before-and-after views.
  • GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile layers, an interactive map file that opens in a browser, and a PDF report in English with maps, the segment table, a thumbnail of each structure and the coordinate register.

Who we work for in the DRC

Mining concessions

Pits, disturbed ground, spoil heaps and structures in and around your perimeter, measured against the art. 279 distances and compared between dates.

ESIA and resettlement

A dated register of structures at the cut-off date, for the census and asset inventory of a resettlement action plan.

Read

For lenders and E&S teams. Dated structure registers support your census and asset inventory and the cut-off-date record that IFC Performance Standard 5 and the World Bank’s ESS5 expect. They do not replace the census. Congolese ESIA rules also ask for “l’inventaire précis et détaillé de l’état initial du site”, a precise and detailed inventory of the site’s initial state (Décret n° 14/019, art. 19), and a dated register feeds straight into it.

Each has its own page: power-line emprises, rail and road emprises, mining perimeters and resettlement cut-off dates.

Satellite first

Documented remotely, with no site access and no overflight

A satellite survey needs neither access to the site nor a flight over it. It starts from your route or boundary file and satellite imagery, open building datasets or the imagery you already hold, and documents how an emprise or a perimeter changes across several dates. All of the analysis is done remotely.

Where teams can no longer reach part of a site, satellite imagery still shows what has changed since the last visit. Re-surveys follow a schedule agreed with you, with a notice after each one; how often depends on the imagery available and on cloud cover.

Where satellite imagery is not enough, a drone survey can be carried out by an eligible Congolese operator, subject to the approvals and security clearances each job requires, starting with the prior authorisation of the Autorité de l’Aviation Civile (AAC) under art. 58 bis of the civil aviation law.

Drones in the DRC

No drone may fly over the country or be operated there without the AAC’s prior authorisation, whatever its weight. The texts, the prohibited zones and a checklist for clients:

Drone law in the DRC

Working with us in the DRC

A technology supplier, alongside an eligible Congolese company

Subcontracting in the DRC is reserved to Congolese-owned companies with their registered office in the country (Loi n° 17/001 of 8 February 2017, amended by Loi n° 26/017 of 30 June 2026), unless the subcontracting regulator, ARSP, grants a derogation. AfriScan therefore works in the DRC as a technology supplier to an eligible Congolese company that holds the contract: the prime contractor carries the contract, and AfriScan supplies the image analysis and the registers.

Each proposal sets out the arrangement for your contract and the documents available. Subcontracting in the DRC, for procurement teams

Our standard

Land and assets, never people

AfriScan records what is on the land: structures, pits, disturbed ground, tracks and vegetation. We do not identify, count or follow people, and whether a structure is authorised is for you and the competent authorities to decide. Our registers support your land, social, legal and community processes; they replace none of them.

An analyst checks every result

Detection models and building datasets propose; an analyst confirms, corrects and adds before any result reaches you.

Dated and credited

Every report names its imagery and, where the source provides it, the capture date. Online map-service basemaps are never passed off as survey imagery.

Scheduled surveys

Satellites and drones capture images on particular dates, so each re-survey follows a schedule agreed with you, with a change notice after it.

Your data stays yours

No route, image or result is published without your written permission, and the registers carry no names of people.

Where we do not work

Provinces outside our scope

For security and public-health reasons we accept no work of any kind, by satellite, by drone or in the field, in North Kivu, South Kivu, Ituri, Haut-Uélé, Bas-Uélé, Tshopo, Maniema, Tanganyika, Haut-Lomami, Sud-Ubangi, Kwilu or Kwango, in the Kwamouth territory, or within 50 km of the border with the Central African Republic.

The list follows the travel advice of the UK government and the French Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs, and the provinces affected by the Ebola disease outbreak reported by the WHO and by France, as checked on 27 September 2026.

Elsewhere in the country

  • Haut-Katanga and Lualaba are served remotely, by satellite.
  • No drone flights near military sites, borders or airports, or over occupied or contested areas.
  • Any field work is carried out by an eligible Congolese company.

Frequently asked questions

Which widths do you measure?

The ones you set, up to six in one survey. Congolese texts give several: 25 m on each side of a high-voltage line and 5 to 50 m for a railway depending on its category (Arrêté interministériel n° 0021 of 29 October 1993), and 800 m and 1,000 m around land a mining right holder plans to occupy (Mining Code art. 279). Your contract, your lender or your own standard may set others; send them with the route.

Do you need site access or a drone flight?

No. A satellite survey starts from your route or boundary file and satellite imagery, so nobody needs access to the site and nothing flies over it. Drone detail is added only where a stretch needs it, carried out by an eligible Congolese operator subject to the approvals and security clearances each job requires, including the AAC’s prior authorisation. See drone law in the DRC.

How recent is the imagery?

It depends on what exists for your area and what the survey is for. Every report names its imagery and, where the source gives it, the capture date. When the date matters, for a cut-off date or a comparison between two dates, we work from dated imagery: a satellite scene acquired for the project, a drone survey, or georeferenced imagery you already hold.

Can you tell us whether a structure is authorised?

No. We record what stands on the ground and when it first appears in the imagery. Whether a structure is authorised, predates the emprise or is covered by an agreement is for you and the competent authorities to decide. The register gives them a dated, located list to work from.

What language are the reports in?

PDF reports are delivered in English. The GIS files (GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile) open in QGIS, ArcGIS and Google Earth, and the interactive map file opens in a web browser. This site also has pages in French.

Do you work in every province?

No. For security and public-health reasons we accept no work in North Kivu, South Kivu, Ituri, Haut-Uélé, Bas-Uélé, Tshopo, Maniema, Tanganyika, Haut-Lomami, Sud-Ubangi, Kwilu or Kwango, in the Kwamouth territory, or within 50 km of the border with the Central African Republic. See where we do not work.

Do you publish our routes or results?

No. We never publish a client’s route, imagery or results without written permission. The sample on this site, a high-pressure gas pipeline in Mozambique, is shown with the route owner’s permission.

Know what stands in your emprise before it becomes a dispute.

Send the line or rail route, or the perimeter boundary (KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile, GPX or GeoPackage), the province and the distances to measure. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
